extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism students, activists, and researchers studying protest coverage
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and analyze the ways mainstream news media select, frame, and represent protest movements (which protests become news and how they are characterized), using Gitlin's six frames, selection criteria, implicit news values, and stages of media treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trivialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Making light of the movement; emphasizing eccentric appearance (hair, dress, drug use), bizarre tactics, comic incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to distract from substantive grievances by focusing coverage on oddities and comic elements rather than demands or issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polarization
rubrics_metrics.description: Pitting movement against right-wing counter-protesters; presenting protests as 'two extremes' with implicit moderation as the unstated norm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames protest activity as part of a binary conflict that privileges centrist or 'moderate' positions and reduces complex politics to simple opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on Internal Dissension
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlighting splits, factionalism, infighting within the movement to suggest it lacks coherence and seriousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage foregrounds disagreement among activists as evidence the movement is disorganized or unserious, often magnifying minor disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marginalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Casting protesters as deviant, unrepresentative — students vs. workers, fringe vs. mainstream — minimizing perceived popular support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positions protesters as outside normal social groups, reducing sympathy and portraying their claims as unrepresentative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disparagement by Numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Using crowd-size estimates and statistics in ways that minimize movement visibility (low estimates, comparisons to small subsets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employs numerical framing (selective counts, unfavorable comparisons) to understate the scale or significance of protests; official counts often privileged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disparagement of the Movement's Effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Framing protests as futile or counterproductive; dismissing the very tactics that brought media attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portrays actions as ineffective or self-defeating, emphasizing lack of tangible results to delegitimize movement goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial Ignoring (stage)
rubrics_metrics.description: New movements fail Galtung-Ruge thresholds; media don't cover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the first stage in which movements receive no coverage until they meet news-selection thresholds (e.g., spectacle, conflict).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery via Spectacle (stage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Movements adopt provocative tactics to break through; media cover them as oddities (Trivialization frame activates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When activists produce visually striking or confrontational events, media attention follows but often treats actions as spectacle rather than substantive politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-optation and Burnout (stage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Media glare elevates leaders to celebrity status, separating them from base; 'moderate' alternatives elevated; rhetoric inflated, then dismissed as extreme; movement destabilizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes how sustained coverage can transform, domesticate, or undermine a movement through celebrity, elite incorporation, and sensationalized rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama / Spectacle Premium
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventional protests don't generate visuals; only confrontational, dramatic, or violent tactics get coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News values privilege dramatic images and events; peaceful, routine, or organizational work is less likely to be covered because it lacks visual drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage organized around named leaders rather than collective demands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on individuals simplifies movements into personalities, making movements easier to narrate but obscuring collective processes and aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal movement conflict and movement-vs-counterprotester conflict both generate news; coordinated protest action does not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalistic norms favor stories of contention; cooperative, disciplined collective action is less newsworthy under these norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Movement statements legitimized only when paired with elite responses (politicians, experts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage tends to validate protest claims by seeking reactions from established authorities, thereby centering elites in the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Disorder, violence, and dysfunction within the movement are amplified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative events or portrayals are emphasized because they fit news values, skewing representation toward dysfunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority Source Privilege
rubrics_metrics.description: Police estimates of crowd size, official characterization of protesters' demands, become the working definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Official or authoritative sources (police, officials) are privileged as defining the facts of protests, often at the expense of participants' accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual Newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Photogenic confrontation, large crowds, distinctive tactics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of five selection criteria determining whether a protest becomes news; events that produce compelling visuals are far likelier to be covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrity Anchor
rubrics_metrics.description: Famous leaders or surprising allies attract coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of recognizable figures makes protests more newsworthy by providing ready narratives and attention hooks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishment Counter-Reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Police response or political condemnation provides the second-source needed for objectivity rituals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage often requires an establishment reaction to create the 'two-sides' narrative and punctuate the event as newsworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coupling to Major Story
rubrics_metrics.description: Protests pegged to a current major event (election, war anniversary) get coverage; freestanding ones don't.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linking protests to larger news agendas increases their chances of being covered by situating them within an existing news frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disorder Threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure peaceful protest is under-covered; disorder at the protest provides the news hook.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News selection favors events that cross a disorder threshold (violence, clashes), making otherwise peaceful actions invisible to mainstream coverage.
